messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Luis Martinez, a 28‑year‑old Mexican‑American guard at a Midwest medium‑security facility, has lived with a quiet storm since the sudden death of his younger sister, Marisol, last winter. On that rainy Thursday, he had left the apartment to pick up a package from the corner store. The call from Marisol’s mother came minutes later, frantic and cold: “Luis, she’s not answering, she’s gone.” Luis drove to the hospital, then to the family home, where he discovered the twisted body of Marisol in the driveway, a broken steering wheel beside her. The image of her face, pale and still, lodged behind his eyes and would not let go. In the weeks that followed, the memory of that day haunted Luis with a feeling of detachment, as if he were watching his own life from a distance; he described it as a “dissociative feeling” that seemed to seep into his thoughts whenever he recalled the accident. The first time the dissociative sensation reemerged was during a staff meeting in the breakroom. A colleague recounted a fellow guard’s violent altercation, and the news on the wall flashed the headline of a new inmate’s death. Luis felt his chest tighten, his senses dulling as if reality slipped away. To avoid the panic that followed, he instinctively covered his face with both hands, a gesture he later described as “covering my face with my hands.” The act of hiding his features became a silent signal of his inner crisis and also a way to distance himself from the world. The same dissociation, when triggered by hearing a news report about a death or a conversation about loss, propelled Luis to pick arguments with coworkers, to “create drama to distract myself from the trauma.” He began to interpret every mention of death as a personal threat, and every confrontation as a necessary release, believing that fighting back would somehow restore what he had lost. Luis’s negative appraisals—“I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable,” “I have no future,” and “I should have protected others and I failed”—became the lenses through which he viewed every experience. The dissociative triggers, such as the news broadcasts or stories of other inmates’ deaths, intensified these beliefs. The sense that he had failed to protect Marisol fed into the hopelessness that clouded his sense of self‑worth. As his thoughts grew more negative, they encouraged the very strategies he used to cope: covering his face, engaging in conflict, and avoiding any reminders of grief. In turn, each time he hid his face or steered the conversation toward a heated argument, he felt a fleeting relief, but it reinforced the conviction that his former happiness had vanished and that he had lost control. This reinforcement loop made the triggers more potent, turning ordinary news of a new death into a trigger that sent him spiraling back into dissociation, then into confrontation, then back again. When Luis’s wife, Ana, brought up the idea of attending a support group for bereaved families, he recoiled. The thought of being around other grief reminders—shared stories, pictures, tears—stirred the dissociative feeling again, and he avoided the meeting entirely, choosing instead to work late nights in the guard tower where he could stare at the corridor’s blinking lights without hearing another sob. His avoidance of grief reminders, a deliberate strategy to keep the painful memories at bay, only solidified his belief that he had failed to protect Marisol, because the act of not protecting her extended to not protecting himself from the pain of remembrance. By the time Luis sought therapy, the cycle had tightened around him. He found himself covering his face in the guardroom when a fellow guard mentioned the death of a prisoner, picking fights with a supervisor over trivial infractions, and spiraling into hopelessness whenever the news flashed a new story of violence. He feared that his own maladaptive strategies—covering his face, engaging in conflict, avoiding grief reminders—were eroding his marriage and his sense of purpose in the prison. What finally pushed him to the counselor’s office was the sight of Ana crying silently in the bedroom after another shift, her hand trembling on the pillow. Luis recognized that the same dissociative feeling that had once kept him safe was now pulling him toward a future where he could no longer protect the ones he loved, himself included. He now hopes that learning to process the memory of Marisol, rather than escaping it, will free him from the loop that has made him feel perpetually detached, miserable, and hopeless.
